scenes.narration: What if your skin could photosynthesize, like a leaf? No more grocery runs. Lunch would just mean stepping out into the sunshine.
Subscribe if you like the math, because here it comes.
Bright midday sun delivers roughly a thousand watts per square meter. Stand in it, and about one square meter of you faces the Sun.
The catch: photosynthesis is inefficient. Even in theory, most plants store at most four point six percent of the sunlight they get.
Do the math, and that's about forty food calories an hour, in perfect, cloudless sun.
Six hours of that gives you around two hundred and forty calories. A typical daily guide is two thousand.
To live on light alone, you'd need roughly eight times more skin facing the Sun, all day, every single day.
Yet one animal does a version of this. The sea slug Elysia chlorotica steals chloroplasts from the algae it eats, and keeps them working for months.
And look at its shape: flat, wide and green. To run on sunlight, it basically became a leaf.

claims.claim: Clear-sky peak sunlight is about 1000 W per square metre (standard AM1.5 reference)
Adult body surface area is roughly 1.7-1.9 m², so about 1 m² faces the Sun at once (rough estimate)
Maximum theoretical solar-to-biomass efficiency is 4.6% for C3 plants (most plants), 6% for C4
1000 W/m² x 1 m² x 4.6% = 46 W, about 40 kcal per hour (own calculation from the sourced figures)
Six hours gives about 240 kcal versus the 2,000-calorie daily reference; about 8x the sun-facing area needed (own calculation)
Elysia chlorotica takes up chloroplasts from the alga Vaucheria litorea and keeps them photosynthesizing
Elysia chlorotica's stolen chloroplasts keep photosynthesizing for months (up to its ~10-month lifespan)

meta.title: What If Humans Could Photosynthesize?
meta.summary: Green skin, free lunch? We run the numbers on a sun-powered human, and meet the sea slug that actually steals photosynthesis.
